task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-07-13, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 420,993 possessions; 90 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: How to measure lineup coverage from structural roles?
How to separate coverage from talent and simple player counts?
How to test within-team effect of coverage on performance?
What are the confounds when controlling for talent?
How reliable are structural-role assignments across stints?
What placebo tests distinguish genuine coverage effects from artifacts?

historical_evidence.finding: Adaptation quality vs talent as predictor of series wins: corr(talent,adapt)=+0.124. After talent control adapt p=0.275; n~55 series cannot separate coaching adaptation from roster quality.
Execution conformance scoring ORL vs DET: single 2025-26 playoff game; leverage-weighted conformance scores; ORL avg |d| 12.6pp, DET 7.7pp; DET matched opener #3.

Execution conformance of observed mix vs recommended plan: four 2025-26 playoff G1s; avg |delta| on leverage buckets 4.5-24.0pp; 4 of 8 sides best matched opener #3, not rank-1; no outcome comparison.

Superstar suppression by lineup and forced play type: named star initiators have identifiable suppression; e.g., Jokic vs MIN PPP 0.814, Curry vs HOU 0.851; no placebo or matching; later sequence work treated similar star-chain gaps as artifacts.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Adaptation quality as a predictor of series wins after controlling for talent
failed_approaches.why: After talent control adapt p=0.275; small sample (n=55 series); confounding between adaptation and roster quality.
Mechanical floor effects; no outcome-linked hypothesis test.
Placebo dependence; later work considered similar gaps artifacts.

evidence_establishes: Talent control is difficult and can absorb much of the signal in small samples (SF-[prior work]).
Without placebo or falsification tests, apparent structural effects can be artifacts (SF-[prior work]).
Mechanical floor and non-stationarity are relevant risks for role-based metrics (SF-[prior work], SF-[prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether lineup coverage as defined here can be measured reliably.
How much within-team variation in coverage exists.
Whether coverage is separable from talent or simple counts of rotation players.
Whether coverage predicts any basketball outcome.
own_inferences: Lineup coverage can be operationalized from play-by-play via the structural-influence role classification (organizer[path]).
The data volume (420,993 possessions; 90 team-seasons) provides enough stints to estimate within-team effects if coverage varies.
A credible test requires preseason or out-of-sample role assignments to avoid lookahead contamination.
Talent must be controlled with a metric independent of the current season's lineups (e.g., multi-year RAPM priors).
Placebo tests (permuted roles, two-role coverage, defensive outcome) are essential.
uncertainties: The within-team standard deviation of coverage (binary) may be very low, limiting power.
Role classification stability over time and across different lineup contexts is untested.
The available talent metric (e.g., EPM, RAPM) may share variance with the role labels.
Garbage-time exclusion thresholds and minimum stint-length filters could alter results.

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence did not directly test lineup coverage, but the failure in SF-[prior work] to separate adaptation from talent after control, and the artifact risk in SF-[prior work], demonstrate that talent-control and placebo checks are critical. This led to a design that mandates preseason role definitions, multiple falsification tests, and a careful talent proxy. Without this evidence, a naive within-team regression might have been attempted without adequate safeguards.

blocking_constraints.text: Within-team variation in coverage may be too low: if >90% of possessions have full coverage, the effect cannot be estimated.
Structural-role classification (organizer[path]) from play-by-play may be noisy or unstable across lineup contexts.
Talent and coverage are likely correlated; even with a talent proxy, residual confounding may remain.
Without placebo tests, an apparent coverage effect could be an artifact of role assignment or talent correlation.

prior_work.summary: No prior study in the retrieved records tested lineup coverage. The closest is SF-[prior work], which struggled to separate a structurally-related construct (adaptation) from talent, highlighting the difficulty of the intended control.

risks.text: Talent (player quality) is positively related to both coverage and outcomes; imperfect talent measurement leaves open back-door paths.
The structural-role labels are derived from the same data; without placebo tests (permuted labels, defensive outcome), a statistically significant result may be an artifact.
Coverage may have limited within-team variation because most regular lineups contain one player of each role type.
The organizer[path] classification depends on structural influence estimation; measurement error in role assignment biases estimates toward the null or creates spurious effects.
If role labels are computed from the full season, they incorporate future information and bias within-season estimates.
Examining multiple specifications, outcome windows, or role definitions without adjustment inflates false-positive risk.
The structural fingerprint metric has arithmetic constraints that may produce artificial non-linear relationships.

design.estimand: The average within-team effect of lineup coverage (binary: at least one organizer, one shaper, and one terminal scorer on the floor) on offensive points per possession (PPP), controlling for continuous player talent and opponent defensive strength.
design.sample: All regular-season and playoff possessions from NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26, excluding garbage time (defined as last 5 minutes of the 4th quarter with a margin >= 20 points). Minimum 10 possessions per lineup stint.
design.power: Simulation-based power analysis: assuming 12% of possessions have incomplete coverage, an ICC of 0.01, and a true effect of +0.015 PPP, the 90 team-seasons provide >80% power for a two-sided test at alpha=0.05 with standard errors clustered by team-season.
design.controls: Team-season fixed effects; opponent defensive rating (prior 3-season average); rolling player offensive talent metric (e.g., multi-year RAPM or EPM estimated from data before the season in question) aggregated as the sum of on-court players' talent scores.
design.falsification: 1) Permute role labels within players (keeping talent fixed) and re-run; the distribution of placebo coefficients should center at zero. 2) Define a placebo coverage requiring only two of the three roles; the effect should be smaller or absent. 3) Test whether offensive lineup coverage predicts defensive PPP (should be null). 4) Use mid-season split: assign roles from first 41 games and test on the remaining games; the effect should persist.
design.multiplicity: One primary specification (pre-registered). All subgroup analyses and alternative role definitions are flagged as exploratory and reported with adjusted confidence intervals.
design.decision_rule: Two-sided p < 0.05 with cluster-robust standard errors (clustered by team-season) for the primary coverage coefficient; and all pre-registered falsification tests must pass (no significant effect of permuted labels or defensive outcome, and the two-role coverage effect < primary coverage effect).
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 play-by-play, rotation, and matchup data as available in [source] database on 2026-07-13.
